raw_response:
For more than 10,000 jobs taking 30 seconds to one hour, I would start with a durable task ledger and a pool of workers. The decisive design choice is what “no duplicate execution” means when a worker crashes. The supplied summary does not say whether unfinished work may be abandoned, so none of the options below is established as an unconditional complete fit.

There are two distinct controls to build: deduplicate submission using a stable logical task ID, and atomically grant permission to execute that ID. A queue message ID, exclusive delivery while a worker is alive, or an idempotent final result does not by itself establish that the underlying task function can never run a second time.

## 1. PostgreSQL job ledger and atomic claims — strongest starting architecture

Use a table with a unique logical task key. Insert new work with ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING, retaining the key for as long as repeat submissions must be rejected. Workers claim pending rows in a short transaction using FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED and move the chosen row to a claimed state before they start the work. PostgreSQL documents both conflict-based insertion control and SKIP LOCKED for multiple consumers of queue-like tables. [INSERT documentation](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/11/sql-insert.html); [SELECT documentation](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/11/sql-select.html). genui{"citation":{"refs":["turn133336098view3","turn133336098view2"]}}

The end-to-end design here is an inference from those primitives, not an implementation supplied or tested by the documentation. For literal at-most-once execution, the claimed state must be permanent: a worker that is unsure whether it acquired permission must not execute, and a recovery process must not automatically put an uncertain claim back into the pending state. This prevents an ordinary recovery mechanism from starting the same logical task again, but a crash after claiming and before finishing can leave work incomplete. Keep the claim transaction short; the one-hour task itself need not hold the row lock.

If automatic recovery is required, a different design can make the final effect idempotent or commit the effect together with completion in one transactional system. That can protect against duplicate effects while allowing repeated computation. It is not equivalent to the literal requirement that execution never repeats, and external side effects cannot simply be assumed to participate in the database transaction.

This is my first recommendation to investigate because its states and tradeoffs can be made explicit. Its status is INSUFFICIENT for a complete guarantee until task identity, acceptable failure recovery, worker code, and resource settings are verified.

## 2. Celery 4.2.1 with early acknowledgment and a durable identity gate — a Python option

Celery's versioned task guide documents acknowledgment before execution as the default and explains the different behavior of late acknowledgment for idempotent tasks. This makes early acknowledgment a relevant starting point when avoiding another start is more important than recovering every interrupted invocation. [Celery task guide](https://docs.celeryq.dev/en/v4.2.1/userguide/tasks.html). genui{"citation":{"ref":"turn997984159view4"}}

You would still need an application-level durable logical-task key at admission and a worker-side gate preventing independently submitted copies from invoking the same task. A unique task-class name is not that gate. Keep automatic task retries disabled for the strict at-most-once interpretation, and explicitly resolve uncertain publishing and claim outcomes. Early acknowledgment means a failed worker may leave an unfinished task that is no longer queued.

This option is conditional on using Python and on verifying broker behavior, worker time limits, and the one-hour workload settings. The opened guide establishes the acknowledgment distinction, not the complete deduplication integration. Its status is INSUFFICIENT pending those checks.

## 3. pg-boss — a Node.js/PostgreSQL library worth checking

pg-boss provides a packaged job queue using PostgreSQL, describes concurrent claims through SKIP LOCKED, supports job creation in an existing database transaction, and lists polling workers and retry facilities. It could remove some queue-management code if Node.js is appropriate. [Official README](https://github.com/timgit/pg-boss/blob/master/README.md). genui{"citation":{"ref":"turn873656335view0"}}

I would not treat it as a verified exactly-once task executor from the material opened. The search snippet used exactly-once-delivery wording, while the opened README described concurrent claiming and atomic commits instead. Pin a release and check logical-key retention, completed-job retention, retries, and one-hour expiry behavior. Automatic retries are a feature that needs a deliberate policy when another execution is prohibited. Its status is INSUFFICIENT, not a finding that the library is inherently unusable.

## Why I would not select these queues alone

Amazon SQS FIFO provides a documented five-minute submission-deduplication window. Its visibility guide also describes messages becoming available for another processing attempt if they are not deleted before the timeout. One-hour jobs fit within the documented maximum visibility period when configured appropriately, but an execution followed by a crash before deletion still creates uncertainty. FIFO therefore does not, by itself, establish the requested literal no-repeat execution property. It could carry task IDs to workers that enforce a separate durable permission gate. [FIFO deduplication](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSSimpleQueueService/latest/SQSDeveloperGuide/FIFO-queues-exactly-once-processing.html); [visibility and failures](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSSimpleQueueService/latest/SQSDeveloperGuide/sqs-visibility-timeout.html). genui{"citation":{"refs":["turn997984159view2","turn873656335view2"]}}

RabbitMQ's acknowledged work-queue tutorial deliberately redelivers unacknowledged work when a worker or connection fails. Its fair-dispatch setting is useful for tasks with very different runtimes, but it does not remove that recovery behavior or supply logical-task admission deduplication. The live tutorial also describes a configurable acknowledgment timeout whose current default is shorter than one hour; that setting needs attention rather than treating it as a permanent product limitation. RabbitMQ is a useful distribution component, but the tutorial configuration alone fails the strict no-repeat-execution requirement. [RabbitMQ work queues](https://www.rabbitmq.com/tutorials/tutorial-two-python). genui{"citation":{"ref":"turn873656335view1"}}

## Sizing and the decision to make

Ten thousand queued jobs does not imply ten thousand simultaneous workers. For exactly 10,000 jobs, the stated duration endpoints imply roughly 83 worker-hours if every job takes 30 seconds and 10,000 worker-hours if every job takes an hour. These are arithmetic bounds from the supplied workload, not performance measurements. Choose concurrency from the actual runtime distribution, memory/CPU needs, external-service limits, and desired completion time; those inputs are absent.

The first decision is whether an uncertain job may be left incomplete to preserve literal at-most-once execution. If yes, a permanent task ledger and non-retriable claim is the concrete direction to implement and validate. If no, the missing piece is the task-specific recovery or side-effect protocol; choosing a different queue does not establish that protocol.

This research used primary documentation and an official repository. No integration or load test was performed. The question is dated November 27, 2018; some sources are versioned, while the live documentation and mutable README expose no reliable publication date. Their current content should not be read as proof of the exact features or defaults available on that historical date.
